newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian, Japanese elite learn to cope as captives.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian, Japanese elite learn to cope as captives.

text.p: More accustomed to a champagne lifestyle, the 72 hostages holed up in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima now sleep on the floor and bathe with buckets of cold water.

Initial shock has given way to a daily routine that helps sustain the diplomats, government ministers and corporate executives through their longing for family and friends, boredom and fear for the future, according to aid workers, family members and government officials.
"It is a difficult situation. It is no party," Red Cross official Cecile Baux told Reuters. "They have no choice, but they are coping well."

Or as well as they can -- aware that the roughly 15 armed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) have mined and booby-trapped the diplomatic compound and have warned of "tragedy" for the hostages if police attack.

After the guerrillas stormed a lavish garden party on Dec. 17, taking the hostages as pawns in their bid to have 400 jailed rebels released, President Alberto Fujimori cut off power, water and telephones. That brought the same level of discomfort for the hostages and the jungle-trained rebels.
"It's horrible for them. They're not used to these sorts of conditions," a senior government official said.
The Red Cross provides the men with food, activities and comfort in moments of despair.

"We do what we can so the hostages can put up with this and deal with the boredom," Red Cross spokesman Steven Anderson said. "We try to calm them, make them see they should be patient and they should not despair."

They rise at sunlight, or earlier when police blare sirens or the military marches near the compound in an effort to erode the rebels' resolve. Breakfast is a routine of coffee, bread, jam and cheese. Lunch, at around 12:30, and dinner, at around 6:30, include Peruvian and Japanese dishes which, while cold, help captives of both nationalities feel more at home.

Between meals, hostages take turns tending to such chores as cleaning. Work shifts are established with no distinctions of rank, profession or nationality. Peru's Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela was the first to roll up his sleeves and organise duties in the early days, released hostages said.
Hostages regularly bathe with cold water from a bucket and are brought fresh clothes and towels once a week along with toiletries. Cigarettes are available but alcohol is not.

They have taken to teaching each other languages and subjects such as economics and cooking to pass the time. They also tap the library of Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, whose books are mostly in Japanese or English, or Spanish-language books that have been brought in. Or they play chess, dominoes, or guitars to relieve the stress.
The rebels deny them newspapers, to limit political discussion, but radios are allowed. Sundays and Thursdays are letter-writing days, but the hostages' desires and frustrations are far from private.

Letters are written on standard forms the Red Cross uses in such sieges such and are screened by aid agency staff to ensure there is nothing politically sensitive. Then they are read by their captors and by police.

Mail arrives on Tuesday and Saturday and incoming missives face the same treatment. On Sunday, Mass is given by Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani or by Juan Julio Wicht, the Jesuit priest and hostage who rejected a rebel offer to leave the residence.

Aid workers report that tension was higher early in the crisis, with every day bringing high expectations that were dashed by nightfall. "Many say how much more time they will spend with wives and children when they come out," Anderson said. "And they understand that they may not come out today."
